en: A great upheaval cast upon the world.
Lion born of Akbaltai,
My lion, watch over us.
Offspring of the lion-hearted hero,
From this present grievous turmoil
Come and deliver us.
Agybai, son of the Argyn khan,
White-browed champion who entered the fray,
Noble-browed gray wolf among all.
You knew the tongues of sixty tribes,
Broad of jaw and fluent of tongue,
You were a hero who never faltered.
Sent ahead, you brought good fortune;
Leading the way, you were like a myriad troops,
You were one of the gray-wolf heroes.
You were the dark eye of the gray wolves,
You were nobility itself.
Watch over us,
Protect my child.
Each of you was a living hero:
Yrchy-uul of the Katagan,
And valiant Shuutu in his felt-cap;
Tölöchü, son of Tölöman,
The darling of your four households;
Baichoro, son of Baabedin,
Watch over us.
All of the forty companions,
Their elder, led by Kyrgyl,
Remain his comrades!”
So mighty Bakai spoke,
Shouting out his blessing,
Stirring the whole world,
And calling upon the spirits
Of the companions gone to the next world.
His face grew pale and drawn,
And tears streamed from both eyes,
Pouring down upon his breast.
“Wretched, meaningless world!” he said,
And sought refuge in the warrior maiden,
Slung his prayer-pouch around his neck,
And pleaded with the Creator:
“May the Maker grant us favor!”
In his old age, Bakai’s
Heart burned and grieved.
A man’s deafness is a bitter thing,
Leaving him no better than the black earth.
It was wise of Almighty God, who created us,
Not to let life linger overlong,
But to take it away.
The burden of years is a snare,
A living head is brought to shame.
It was wise to take a man
Before leaving him utterly feeble.
Allah Almighty, the one God,
What did He intend for His living servant?
Yesterday, in my blue-lynx and sable cap,
When I strode with a swagger,
When I ruled as khan over the wide world
And lived in joy,
Why did I not die then, before seeing
The misery of this strange world?
Why did I not die here
While my glorious fame endured,
Before they called me sorrowful Bakai?
When life burst from my voice,
Dust rose beneath my tread,
Blood streamed from my sword,
And lament rose over those dear to me;
When my words laid the world
As desolate as a desert;
When I held dominion
Over the whole wide world;
When anyone who defied me,
Or ventured too near,
I struck down;
When I made this world my slave
And held it bound;
When I hemmed in hostile Kakan
From every side;
When I made the world resound with blows,
Beating it into submission—
Why did I not die then?
My chest rattles,
My eyes are festering;
Sixty sinews and eighty bones
Tremble, finding no remedy.
The guiding thought has left me,
My tall, plane-tree stature is gone;
The cords of my eyes are severed,
Courage has fled my breast,
And I have come to the point of death.
The black earth, deep as a bowl,
Will not stir as I am made
To endure this misery.
Old age has come and laid me low;
Skill has left these cherished hands,
The blazing strength has left my arms,
Power, courage, and vigor
Have vanished utterly, leaving nothing.
With a bleached skull for my pillow
And my head turned toward the qibla,
I cannot die though I long for death,
Nor can my proud and precious soul
Bring my hand to end it.
Like spring water flowing down a hill,
My joints fail, and I cannot gather myself.
Tasseled quiver and ornate arrow—
While youth still remained,
I filled the world with tales;
Now I have no fortune left to display.
Fatherly child, Kuyaly,
Though you may now enter the struggle,
My spirit holds countless cares;
That cherished strength like a blue flame,
However much I wish for it, is gone.
This is the hour when age drives courage away,
When ordinary, crumbling earth
Covers the cherished soul.
My mind remains, but I have no means;
Everyone’s turn comes one day—
Damn this filthy world!
My darkened eyes have filmed over;
My two hands, once fearless before the world,
Hang paralyzed and cannot rise.
My whole body has grown numb,
Every joint is constricted,
And dropsy has left every limb
Unable to stir.
All torments have come upon me;
I long to die, but cannot,
And before God, whose decree is stern,
I cannot walk there by myself.
Thus, through old age,
My time of ruin has come.
Courage has fled my breast;
My time of utter emptiness has come.
When I was drunk with liquor,
When youth cultivated wisdom,
When a fierce battle-frenzy seized me,
I would bring dreadful strife
Upon the warring Chinese.
Thus would I raid and conquer
Kakan, stricken by slaughter.
The ways that once were mine
Have become strange to me.
I have reached the hour
When I must cease to be.
Bakai stood there distraught,
Spread his palms, and prayed.
Your uncle Bakai, the gray wolf,
Your forefather who had seen so much,
His eyes had become blind,
His ears deaf,
And the poor man remained
No better than the black earth.
Burdened with grievous suffering,
Though only yesterday he held sway
Over all the teeming multitude,
The aged gray wolf Bakai
Had once charged like a blue wolf.
In the beginning, your forefather Bakai
Was mighty throughout the whole world;
Yet at another time, mighty Bakai
Was humbled into tending camels.
Spreading his hands and saying, “Amen,”
Dear Bakai collapsed;
Desolating old age
Struck him down and let him rise no more.
These were the lofty honors
Of your aged forefather Bakai:
Though mortal, Bakai’s living spirit endured;
Upon your prophet-like forefather
A golden crown was placed,
And the golden throne left by Manas
Was mounted by Khan Bakai.
Endless fortune and broad pastures
Were inscribed upon the brow
Of an elder such as Bakai.
When Bakai fell,
Your dear mother Kanykei
Sprang to action like a hawk;
The venerable lady herself
Suddenly found a plan.
Arming herself with the jezail,
She appealed to Kuyaly,
The lionhearted warrior daughter of Kaiypchal,
And began her speech at length,
Speaking softly but with firm resolve.
Your fierce, ill-fated mother,
Most graceful of the long-haired,
Mightiest among women,
Purest of those in flowing gowns,
The foremost of womankind—
Such was that blessed soul,
Deeply wondrous and rich in wisdom.
Her eyes were Venus, her tongue was honey;
No such soul is born among humankind.
The venerable woman who bore a hero
Was a saint among women.
Her words were sweet, her tongue was honey;
However long you speak, none like her appears.
Such was the sacred power
Of your dear mother, the venerable lady:
She joined together what was severed
And gathered what was scattered.
At night her treasure-chests loomed like mountains;
While her gray-wolf mountain yet stood,
Her command reached across the world.
Your noble mother Kanykei
Spoke plainly while alive,
And kept her eyes open until death.
Your dear and noble mother
Said this to the warrior maiden,
Telling her child a wondrous secret:
“Warrior maiden, my child Kuyaly,
When I still possessed sacred power,
When I once surged like fire
And flourished in my prime,
When abundant wealth and great fortune
Still bade me journey on,
On the Night of Destiny in the holy week,
I lay down and dreamed a dream:
Its collar was fine and its tether golden—
In my dream I caught a falcon.
Saying it would accompany the lion’s son,
I tethered it fast and secure.
Then, through God’s mysterious doing,
Barefoot and bareheaded,
Named Khizr and noble in essence,
An old, white-bearded dervish
Appeared before me.
The white-bearded one came and said:
‘The towering golden Ala-Too
Cannot be overrun by an invading foe,
Nor seized by any man who marks it well.
Until the end of time,
Here is the land where descendants
Will have their soiled shirts washed,
And the blood of their birth-cords staunched;
This is the land where they shall remain.
Its country is blissful, its people well-fed,
A people of unmatched boldness in the world,
Open-handed and generous with all they have—
Such are the fortunate Kyrgyz people.
If you find its strength, this is your nation;
Yet sorrow lies within your breast.
Dark-hearted and blue-clad,
Immeasurable Semetey—
Such is the son you are to bear.
When you give birth to the child,
Forty envoys from China
Will come, feast at his celebration, and depart.
If this son survives,
They will say he shall overturn the age.
Ten envoys from Russia
Will also feast and depart.
